title: Current Density: A/cm², A/mm² and A/in²
h1: Current density units — A/cm², A/mm² and A/in²
description: 1 A/mm² = 100 A/cm² = 645 A/in². PCB traces run 20 A/mm². Motor windings hit 5 A/mm² continuous, 15 A/mm² short-term.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: Current density sets the temperature rise. Miss the unit and copper melts.
body: Current density (A per unit area) is what actually heats a conductor. Different disciplines use different area units, and the factors are not friendly numbers.

> 1 A/mm² = 100 A/cm² = 10⁶ A/m² = 645.16 A/in²
> 1 A/cm² = 6.452 A/in²
> 1 A/in² = 0.00155 A/mm²

Copper wire in still air (residential): 3–5 A/mm². Copper wire in cable trays: 2–3 A/mm². Motor windings (Class F, continuous): 4–6 A/mm². PCB internal trace: 20 A/mm² for short lengths. Electroplating cathodes: 0.01–0.1 A/cm².

A rewind spec says 5 A/mm² for continuous duty. A 100 A motor needs 20 mm² of copper — 4 mm × 5 mm strap, or 26 turns of AWG 6 magnet wire. Miscopy the spec as 5 A/cm² and you install 2000 mm² of copper — 100× oversized, physically impossible.
A/mm² and A/cm² differ by 100. Match the unit on the datasheet.

faqs.a: Temperature rise. Insulation class, cooling, and duty cycle all shift the limit.
Yes — solid bar dissipates heat over larger surface area. Typical values 1.5–3 A/mm² for continuous.
